howTo: Enter the thermal conductivity k of the material (W/m·K). For reference: steel ≈ 45–50, aluminium ≈ 160–210, copper ≈ 385, concrete ≈ 0.8–1.4.
Enter the cross-sectional area A (m²) perpendicular to heat flow, the temperature difference ΔT (K or °C) across the material, and the thickness L (m) in the direction of heat flow.
The tool returns steady-state heat flow rate Q (W) and thermal resistance R (K/W). Verify that all inputs share consistent SI units before drawing engineering conclusions.
formula: Q = k · A · ΔT / L | R = L / (k · A) | Q = ΔT / R

examples.title: Steel wall, industrial furnace panel
examples.description: Estimating steady-state heat loss through a 10 mm thick mild-steel plate at a face temperature difference of 30 K.
notes: Q = 45 × 0.02 × 30 / 0.01 = 2700 W. Verify the thermal conductivity value against the actual material grade and operating temperature.
This is a one-dimensional, steady-state approximation. Edge effects, surface convection, and radiation are not included.

examples.title: Concrete wall, building energy analysis
examples.description: A 200 mm thick concrete wall, 1 m² panel, with a 15 K indoor-outdoor temperature difference.
notes: Q = 1.2 × 1.0 × 15 / 0.2 = 90 W. Real building walls contain multiple layers; use thermal resistance addition (R_total = R1 + R2 + …) for composite walls.
Moisture content significantly affects k for concrete and masonry. Use laboratory-tested or certified values for compliance calculations.

references.title: Fourier's Law of Heat Conduction
references.note: Q = −k A (dT/dx). The tool applies the one-dimensional, steady-state form for a flat plate.

references.title: ISO 10456
references.note: Building materials — Procedures for determining declared and design thermal values. Tabulated k values at reference conditions.

references.title: Incropera & DeWitt — Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer
references.note: Standard textbook reference for conduction, convection, and radiation fundamentals.

commonMistakes: Entering area in cm² instead of m² — this produces a result 10,000 times smaller than the correct value.
Using thickness in mm instead of m — this overstates Q by a factor of 1,000.
Applying the formula to composite multi-layer walls without accounting for individual layer resistances and interface contact resistance.
assumptions: One-dimensional steady-state conduction through a flat, homogeneous slab.
Thermal conductivity k is constant and independent of temperature over the specified range.
Surface heat transfer coefficients (convection, radiation) are not included; the result covers the conduction path only.
